title: AD Replication in Plain English
summary: Replication is how every domain controller tells every other domain controller what changed.
analogy: Think of every domain controller as a branch office of the same bank, all sharing one customer ledger. When one branch updates a balance, it has to tell the other branches - that message-passing is replication. If a branch stops receiving messages, its ledger drifts out of sync with reality.
plain_language_explanation: Any domain controller can accept a change (multi-master). Once it does, that change has to spread to every other domain controller. The tool `repadmin` tells you whether that spreading is happening on schedule or has stalled somewhere.
visual_hint: Use the AD-REPLICATION topology visual (OSB-AD-VISUAL-0001) to see the branch offices as nodes and replication links as arrows.
quick_check: True or false: only one domain controller is allowed to accept changes at a time.

title: FSMO Roles: The Five Special Jobs
summary: Five specific jobs in AD can only be done by one domain controller at a time - these are the FSMO roles.
analogy: Most branch-office decisions (in our bank analogy) can be made by any branch. But a handful of jobs - like approving a brand-new type of account, or being the master clock everyone syncs to - are assigned to exactly one branch, so there's never a conflicting answer.
plain_language_explanation: The five FSMO roles are: Schema Master and Domain Naming Master (one each per entire forest), and PDC Emulator, RID Master, Infrastructure Master (one each per domain). If the DC holding a role goes down permanently, someone must transfer (or, in an emergency, forcibly seize) that role onto a healthy DC.
visual_hint: Comparison visual showing forest-wide vs domain-wide role scope (OSB-AD-VISUAL, future batch).
quick_check: Is the PDC Emulator a forest-wide or domain-wide role?

title: Forest Recovery: The Fire-Escape Plan
summary: Forest recovery is what you do when Active Directory itself is broken everywhere, not just on one server.
analogy: If one branch's computer breaks, you fix that computer. If the entire bank's shared ledger system is corrupted everywhere at once, you go back to the last trusted printed statement and rebuild from there, branch by branch, starting with head office. That full rebuild is forest recovery.
plain_language_explanation: You only do this when every domain controller is unusable or untrustworthy. You restore one clean domain controller per domain from backup - starting with the forest root domain - then carefully bring the rest back one at a time. Anything created or changed after your last backup is gone.
visual_hint: Decision-tree visual for 'do I need forest recovery' (OSB-AD-VISUAL-0003).
quick_check: If only one of your ten domain controllers has a problem, do you need forest recovery?

title: Kerberos in Plain English: Tickets, Not Passwords
summary: Kerberos lets you prove who you are using time-limited tickets instead of sending your password around the network.
analogy: It's like a theme park: you show ID once at the gate and get a wristband (ticket). For the rest of the day, rides just check your wristband, not your ID again - and the wristband expires at closing time.
plain_language_explanation: A domain controller acting as the Key Distribution Center (KDC) issues a ticket after you authenticate once. Services you access afterward just validate that ticket. If your computer's clock is more than about 5 minutes off from the DC's, the ticket looks invalid and you get an error.
visual_hint: Sequence animation of ticket request/grant/use flow (OSB-AD-VISUAL-0002).
quick_check: Why does a badly out-of-sync clock break Kerberos logins?

title: gMSA in Plain English: A Service Account That Changes Its Own Password
summary: A gMSA is a service account that Windows manages for you - including rotating its own password automatically.
analogy: A normal service account is like a shared office key that someone has to physically remember to re-cut every month. A gMSA is a smart lock that quietly reprograms its own key on a schedule - and every authorized door (server) automatically accepts the new key.
plain_language_explanation: Instead of an admin manually resetting a service account's password on a schedule (and syncing it everywhere the service runs), Windows generates and rotates a long, random password every 30 days by default, and every server that's allowed to use the gMSA can fetch the current value automatically.
quick_check: Who manually resets a gMSA's password?
